Pixel Blade · the mark · fresh start

The kerf.

A kerf is the material a blade removes as it passes. That is the whole mark: a solid disc, cut once, the lower piece slid along the cut, and in the gap the material the blade took — as pixels, coarsening and scattering as they leave.

Blades are no longer steel. Pixels.

What changed

I was drawing outlines. None of your references have one.

That was the actual mistake, and it survived four rounds. Every image you sent builds form the same way — adjacent planes at different values, and the edge is simply where two values meet. The rendered origami crane reads as folded paper for exactly that reason. Nothing in it is outlined.

So I threw out the crane, the ensō, the stroke weights, the whole file, and started again with one rule: no strokes. Only planes. Twenty-seven forms across four rounds, all of them built as facets.

Round one · the kills

A pyramid, a pie chart and a torii.

Straight into decor and clip art. The gate was the worst offence — I had written "a torii in the mark would be tourism" into the lexicon myself two hours earlier, and then drew one.

Two survived, and they turned out to be the two things the company actually is: a folded plane, and a cut that becomes pixels.

Round two · the slip

Solid, not stroked.

A disc cut on a diagonal with the pieces displaced. Solid instead of stroked is a completely different weight — it has presence, and it survives far further down the scale than any ring ever did.

Two findings here. A near-equal split reads as a cut; a thin sliver reads as a moon phase. And sliding the piece along the cut rather than across it is what makes it a slip — across just separates the halves and reads as an eclipse.

Rounds three and four · the kerf

Then the blade left something behind.

A cut disc is a cut disc. What makes it this company's cut disc is what the blade is made of — so the gap fills with the material the cut removed, as blocks.

The direction of the run matters more than anything else in the mark. Fine and tight where the cut is still closed, coarsening and scattering as it opens and leaves the silhouette. Run the other way it reads as the cut healing over — which is the exact opposite of the point.

Why this one

Six reasons it survived and the others didn't.

  • It is not a picture of anything

    So it cannot date, and it cannot be read as a bird, a gate, a brush stroke or a badge. Every previous round failed here.

  • It is the thesis, literally

    Something whole, cut, and moved — and the blade that did it is made of pixels. There is no metaphor to explain.

  • Solid means weight

    Four rounds of rings were all line weight and air. This has mass, which is what lets it hold a page.

  • Asymmetric, so it travels

    The slip gives it a direction. A centred symmetrical mark in a circle goes heraldic immediately.

  • The ensō is still in it

    A circle, opened. The Japanese layer as principle rather than as ornament, which is the standing rule.

  • It degrades honestly

    At 16px the grit drops out and leaves a cut disc. Same two-density system as before, but earned by the geometry instead of imposed on it.

Scale

Where the grit goes.

Below about 24px, and in any single-material application, the grit becomes noise — and worse, when the two halves fuse into one silhouette the run out of the top right starts to read as a fuse. So the rule is explicit: grit where there are two values or two depths, quiet everywhere else. Favicon, app icon, embossing, embroidery, a stamp in a video corner — all quiet.

Both modes

Roles hold. Values swap.

Night · bronze on sumi

The slid piece is the raised one, so it is the lighter one. That is the only reason it is lighter — the same single raking light as everything else in the system.

Day · oxide on paper

Oxide and rust take the bronze roles, exactly as the day mode was defined. No redraw, no reversed artwork, no alternate mark.

In the lockup

Pixel Blade.

Wordmark still the unargued round-one proposal. It is now the oldest unexamined thing in the system and it should be next.

Struck

It holds as an object.

Same geometry through strike.py. Note which versions use the grit and which go quiet — the material decides, not the layout.

Open

Your call.

  • Does it read as a cut?

    To me, yes — and not as a moon, a pie chart or a loading spinner, which were the three failure modes I was watching for. But you have fresher eyes.

  • How loud should the grit be?

    Currently seventeen blocks with a modest scatter. It can go finer and nearly invisible, or much louder with blocks tumbling well clear of the disc.

  • The cut angle

    Twenty-eight degrees off horizontal. Steeper reads more aggressive; shallower reads calmer. One number.

  • The aperture is now homeless

    It was the strongest idea in your reference set and this mark cannot carry it. My instinct is that it survives as a site device rather than a logo — the ring as a hole in the homepage with the garden behind it.
